summary: A trie (prefix tree) stores strings along root-to-node paths, one character per edge. Inserting, searching, and prefix-searching a string of length L all take O(L) time regardless of how many strings are stored, which makes tries ideal for autocomplete and dictionaries.

sections.heading: Structure
sections.body: Each node has links to children (an array of 26 for lowercase letters, or a map for larger alphabets) and a flag marking that a word ends here. The root represents the empty prefix.

sections.heading: Insert and search
sections.body: Walk the characters, creating missing nodes on insert. Search succeeds only if the walk completes and the final node's end flag is set.

sections.heading: Prefix queries
sections.body: To test whether any word starts with a prefix, walk the prefix and succeed if all nodes exist (ignore the end flag). To autocomplete, walk the prefix, then depth-first collect every word below that node.

sections.heading: Complexity
bullets: Insert, search, prefix check: O(L) where L is the string length, independent of the number of words.
Space: O(total characters × alphabet size) in the array form; can be large.
No hashing or collision handling needed; keys come out in lexicographic order.

sections.body: Unmark the end flag, then walk back up freeing nodes that have no children and are not the end of another word. Recursion makes this natural.

bullets: Store children in a hash map or sorted list instead of a fixed array.
Compressed (radix/Patricia) trie: merge chains of single-child nodes into one edge labelled with a substring.
Ternary search tries: three-way BST nodes per character, compact and still prefix-friendly.
IP routing tables: a binary trie over address bits implements longest-prefix match.
T9 text prediction and word games.
Longest common prefix of many strings.
Trie supports prefix search and sorted iteration; hash tables do not.
Hash tables use less memory and have better constants for exact lookups.
Trie lookup time depends on key length, not table size.

sections.body: Store integers bit by bit to answer queries like 'maximum XOR with any stored number' in O(bits): at each bit choose the child that gives the opposite bit when possible.

takeaways: Paths from the root spell strings; a flag marks word ends.
Insert, search, and prefix queries are O(L).
Great for autocomplete and longest-prefix problems; memory can be large.
Compressed tries cut memory by merging single-child chains.
